subject: maths

moments.title: On Computable Numbers
moments.body:
Turing, age 24, publishes 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem'. He defines what we now call a Turing machine — a mathematical model of computation — and proves:

1. There exist 'computable' real numbers (those whose digits can be generated by an algorithm).
2. There exist real numbers that are NOT computable (most of them, in fact).
3. The halting problem is undecidable: no algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary program will halt.
4. The Entscheidungsproblem (Hilbert's question on whether mathematical truth is mechanically decidable) is unsolvable.
moments.takeaway: Computation has a mathematical definition. Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem is settled — negatively.

moments.title: Universal Turing machine
moments.body:
Turing introduces the UNIVERSAL Turing machine: a single machine that, given any other machine's description as input, can simulate that machine.

This is the theoretical basis of the modern programmable computer. The CPU of your computer is, in essence, a universal Turing machine.
moments.takeaway: Hardware and software are separated conceptually. A single physical device can run any computable algorithm.

moments.title: Bletchley Park and the Enigma
moments.who: Alan Turing, Gordon Welchman, others — Bletchley Park
moments.body:
Turing is recruited to Bletchley Park during WWII. He designs the Bombe, an electromechanical device for breaking German Enigma ciphers. Building on Polish work (Marian Rejewski had broken early Enigma), Turing's design handles the more complex naval Enigma.

Bletchley Park breaks tens of thousands of intercepts. Historians estimate the work shortened the war by 2-4 years and saved millions of lives.

The work was top secret. It was not revealed until the 1970s.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical computation becomes life-saving wartime engineering. The work stays classified for 30 years.

moments.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
moments.body:
Turing publishes 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' in the philosophy journal Mind. He asks: can machines think?

He proposes the imitation game (Turing test): if a machine can convince a human judge that it's a human in conversation, we should agree it 'thinks'. He predicts a 70% success rate within 50 years.

quote.text: The original question, 'Can machines think?' I believe to be too meaningless to deserve discussion.

moments.takeaway: Turing recasts the question of machine intelligence as a behavioural test. The Turing test becomes iconic.

moments.title: Trial, chemical castration, death
moments.body:
Turing reports a burglary and incidentally reveals his relationship with another man. Homosexual acts are illegal in Britain. He is prosecuted, convicted (1952), and sentenced to chemical castration as an alternative to prison.

The oestrogen injections cause physical and psychological effects. He loses his security clearance — he can no longer work on the cryptographic research he had pioneered.

On 8 June 1954, Turing is found dead in his bed. Cause: cyanide poisoning. A half-eaten apple lies beside him. He is 41. The inquest rules suicide.

Gordon Brown apologised on behalf of the British government in 2009. Queen Elizabeth pardoned Turing in 2013. The 'Alan Turing Law' (2017) pardoned all men convicted under similar legislation.
moments.takeaway: The mathematician whose work was essential to defeating Nazism is destroyed by his own government for his sexuality. He dies at 41.

now.title: Computation today
now.body:
Computers run civilisation. The Church-Turing thesis (Turing 1936, Church 1936) — that anything computable is computable by a Turing machine — has held up empirically over 90 years.

Quantum computation extends what's efficient (Shor's algorithm factors integers exponentially faster than any known classical algorithm), but the set of COMPUTABLE problems is the same.

Large language models pass some versions of the Turing test. Whether they 'think' is hotly debated.
now.open_questions: P vs NP — are there problems for which solutions are easy to verify but hard to find? Will quantum computers break public-key cryptography? What is consciousness, and could a computer have it? How do we govern AI systems that can outperform humans on many cognitive tasks?

reflection: Turing's life is a tragic emblem of mid-20th century Britain. His contributions to the war and to modern computing are immense; his treatment by his own government was monstrous. How does a society make amends for state-sanctioned destruction of its own creative minds? How do we identify whom we are currently destroying, before it's too late?
